briefOverview: Jesus prepares his disciples for persecution and his departure, promising the coming of the Spirit. He assures them their sorrow will turn to joy and that they will have peace and access to the Father in his name.
summary: Jesus warns that his followers will face expulsion and even lethal hostility from those who think they serve God, because such persecutors do not know the Father or the Son. He says his departure is beneficial, since he will send the Comforter (Spirit of truth) who will expose the world’s sin, righteousness, and judgment, guide the disciples into all truth, and glorify Jesus. He speaks of a brief period when they will not see him and then will see him again, turning their sorrow into joy like a mother after childbirth. He promises that, in the coming day, they will ask the Father in his name and receive, because the Father himself loves them for loving and believing in Jesus. After stating plainly that he came from the Father and is returning to the Father, Jesus foretells the disciples’ imminent scattering but affirms he is not alone, for the Father is with him. He concludes by offering peace amid inevitable tribulation, urging courage because he has overcome the world.
externalContext: This chapter belongs to John’s Farewell Discourse (John 13–17), a set of teachings given on the eve of Jesus’ arrest. In first‑century Judaism, synagogue leaders could discipline members, including expulsion, which would have significant social and religious consequences. The Greek term often translated Comforter or Advocate (Paraclete, paraklētos) carried legal and relational connotations of a helper or legal advocate. Early Jesus‑followers faced opposition both within Jewish settings and, later, from Roman authorities; the warning anticipates such pressures without detailing specific later events.
externalReferences: John previously noted fear of synagogue expulsion (John 9:22; 12:42), echoing 16:2. Jesus’ statement that the “prince of this world” is judged recalls earlier mentions of Satan’s defeat (John 12:31; 14:30). The promise of the Spirit continues themes from John 14:16–17 and 15:26, and prayer “in my name” reiterates promises in John 14:13–14 and 15:16. The prediction of the disciples’ scattering reflects Zechariah 13:7, cited in Matthew 26:31 and Mark 14:27, and their later joy at seeing the risen Jesus matches John 20:20. The assurance of overcoming the world resonates with the victory language in 1 John 5:4–5.

sectionTitles.title: Sorrow to joy and final assurance

practicalQuestions: How should I respond when faithfulness leads to exclusion or hostility?
In what concrete ways do I rely on the Spirit’s guidance rather than self‑reliance?
What does praying “in Jesus’ name” mean for the content and motives of my prayers?
Where do I expect sorrow to give way to joy, and how can I endure the “labor” in hope?
How can Jesus’ promise of peace shape my outlook amid unavoidable pressures?
What practices help me remember that the Father himself loves those who love and trust Jesus?
uncertainAreas: The referent of “a little while … you shall see me” likely points to the resurrection appearances, yet some interpreters see layers that include the Spirit’s coming or the final return; the text emphasizes sorrow turning to immediate joy, suggesting the resurrection as primary. The phrase “you shall ask me nothing” (v. 23) can mean either no more questions or no need to petition him directly, which affects how it relates to praying to the Father in Jesus’ name. The precise meaning of the Spirit convicting “of righteousness, because I go to the Father” (v. 10) is debated—whether it vindicates Jesus’ righteousness, exposes the world’s false standards, or both.
